There was also a second control signal originating from the “Grid Side” that steams from the production DERMS platform using a DNP3 signal to control the Sonnen battery energy storage systems (BESS). Improved communications between the sandbox environment and the production environment were slated as a Budget Period 3 activity and, thus, not completed at the time of project termination. The connection between PAC and the USU EVR and microgrid facility relied on the OpenADR integration to send the control signal to USU’s DERs and to receive telemetry reporting back from the facility. OpenADR was used because it provides a standardized way to communicate between a utility and demand-side resources, and it was easily extensible to provide a wide range of event and report types. OpenADR has two major communication modes: pull mode and push mode. In pull mode, an OpenADR client, called a virtual end node (VEN) frequently polls an OpenADR server, called a virtual top node (VTN) to check if the VTN has generated any new demand response events. Conversely, in push mode, the VTN pushes demand response events to the VEN as soon as it creates an event. As shown in the figure above, the connection between the utility and the microgrid used both modes. For the utility’s external connection to the VEN at USU’s microgrid facility, Berkshire Hathaway Energy (BHE) information technology required the use of the push configuration in order to avoid the large number of requests from an external VEN that would occur while using pull mode. However, the VTN connected to OSI’s EMS sandbox deployed at PAC must operate in pull mode. The requirement to use pull mode to connect to the OSI VTN but push mode in order to connect to locations external to the utility (e.g., USU’s microgrid VTN) necessitated the creation of an OpenADR pull-to-push converter which lives on a server at RMP and helps connect the internal pull-VTN and external push-VEN. The pull-to-push converter had two antiparallel directions of data flow. To transmit OpenADR demand response events from the pull-VTN to the push-VEN, the converter had to pull new events frequently from the push-VTN. It did this using a pull-mode VEN. The converter’s pull-mode VEN ran in parallel with a push-mode VTN. When the converter pulled a new OpenADR event from the pull-mode VTN, its pull-mode VEN passed along the event to its push-mode VTN, which in turn pushed the event to USU’s push-mode VEN which was waiting to be pushed for new events. The second role of the pull-to-push converter was to pass telemetry reports from the push-mode VEN at USU to the pull-mode VTN at RMP. This was handled similarly to the process used for passing events in the opposite direction. The push-mode VEN at USU will generate telemetry reports and pass them to the converter’s push- mode VTN at RMP. The converter’s push-mode VTN then wrote the new report to a stack of reports.
